en: Shouting, he gathered his people,
And Kyyaz summoned his whole nation:
His diviners and wise men,
His elders who had seen much,
All those of great knowledge,
His keen-eared heroes,
The heroes who knew many things—
He gathered his far-flung people.
A great abundance of worldly treasure
He firmly committed to the expense.
Among the people stood a tower—
Ask not how magnificent that tower was!
It rose many fathoms high;
In those days, extraordinary indeed
Was the learning of your hero Kyyaz.
From the tower, hero Kyyaz
Roared out a mighty cry,
And to all the vast assembly
He loudly proclaimed the news,
Announcing to the Jediger nation
That Chürök had borne a child:
“Hear me, my countless black-clad people!
The fairy-born Chürök,
Whom I took and bound in wedlock—
I counted every passing day
And recorded each one in writing.
To plunge into festivities,
To play on without tiring,
Traveling by night and resting by day,
The Jediger of the Seven Valleys
Endured bitter hardship.
Upon forty red-tailed camels
They loaded red gold,
Delighting the moon-bright heart.
A white plume broad as a tent
Was displayed upon the forelock
Of a swift steed, stately as a beast.
Driving livestock for the marriage alliance,
They paid homage and feasted on rich butter.
Karachach, daughter of Karakhan,
Poured out wealth and scattered livestock;
She was the wife I chose and took,
Yet from her I saw no offspring.
Snow has passed along the black mountain;
Many kinds of people have passed away,
Beaming as they cherished children.
I have not even a daughter, much less a son;
Longing for a child has tormented me!
Slaughter ninety beasts for the feast.
My wife whom I won in battle,
That graceful infidel,
The fairy-born Aichürök,
Has borne my hero son.
Name my child for me!
Let ninety beasts be slaughtered for his feast,
And let the child be given his name!”
Saying this, hero Kyyaz
Slaughtered ninety fat mares,
And sheep in great abundance,
As well as many fine colts.
Without further talk, they plunged into revelry,
And the people rose in an uproar:
“The hero has fathered a son!”
If you had seen the countless Jediger,
They all rose in jubilation.
The nation gathered and the people surged;
By this reckoning of days,
Since I took the unfortunate woman,
Eleven months have passed.
The child born today—
My people, consider it well—
Has proved to be my own son!
My joyful heart has turned to celebration;
I shall scatter my wealth and hold a feast
For my newborn child.
Think it right, O Jediger;
Joy has entered my heart.
My heart surges and my eyes shine
At the child revealed to me today.
My people, since Kyyaz became Kyyaz,
Since Kyyaz mounted a horse,
Since he grew to manhood as a hero
And became the equal of heroes’ sons,
Since he donned the white coat of mail
And sat proudly upon his horse,
Since he mounted the bay Tootoru
And rode out on raids,
When yesterday’s battle raged fiercely,
Akbermet, daughter of Kaiypkhan—
While nations gathered and peoples were thrown into turmoil,
And many heroes died in the clash—
Was the wife I captured.
I hung an amulet around her neck,
And painted rouge upon her face;
Never speaking words that might wound her heart,
I cherished her tenderly.
Yet from her I saw no child
And never heard an infant cry “maa.”
Karakhan, khan of the Künjüt,
Had a lissome, sun-bright beauty
Who came from that land.
To win that sunlike beauty,
That lovely woman of sweet and fitting speech,
That woman with lustrous black eyes,
To take such a beauty as my wife
And satisfy my longing once,
A bitter enemy appears
In Aichürök’s eyes.
Gathering his nobles and khans,
Hero Kyyaz stood there,
Demanding, “Give me the child.”
Hero Kyyaz continued to ask:
“My moonlike wife Chürök,
The warm heart within my breast,
This alone was my prayer
To Almighty God:
Fairy-born, unfortunate woman,
You have fulfilled my deepest hope;
My poor dear, you have found for me
The child who will brighten my brow.
The spring flowing through the hills,
The young hero who will remain after me—
Bring my son so I may see him,
Open my mouth, and kiss him!
I shall uncover his radiant brow
And press him to my breast.
Calling this child my support,
I shall banish all my sorrow.
To a white-bearded elder,
One who has lived to a great age,
I shall offer entertainment and discourse
And have him name the child!”
Saying this, hero Kyyaz
Raged in fury.
God had struck Kyyaz,
And still he demanded the child.
Before Kyyaz, greatest of the nation,
There was no way to refuse
The newborn infant;
Such is this wretched world.
The unfortunate fairy-born woman wondered,
“What will the infidel do to the child?
How will he bring about his end?”
If he presses the baby to his breast,
May God strike the infidel;
He means to slaughter the tender young one—
Amid all the great festivity.
Hero Kyyaz, strutting like a cock,
Clasped his hands behind his back.
He would not leave the child alone,
Yet he was somewhat afraid
Of Aichürök’s wrath.
Uttering no words and saying nothing,
Hero Kyyaz stood thinking:
The child was his enemy,
Would take vengeance without fail,
And wage war on a vast scale.
If the orphan lived to grow,
He would take revenge and destroy him;
They would gird themselves for combat
And batter one another to pieces.
Hero Kyyaz knew this;
He knew the child would be his doom.
Burning and blazing like an ember,
He restrained himself only
For fear of frail Chürök.
That day hero Kyyaz
Simply brooded in anguish,
Then into Aichürök’s presence
Kyyaz came running.
To the moonlike woman Chürök,
Into her burden of deep torment,
To the fairy-born unfortunate woman,
Kyyaz rushed in.
Laughing with false words,
The wretch spoke with his lips alone,
Fawning falsely upon the child,
Intending to take the baby in his hands,
To have him named,
Then, while the child was still an infant,
To gouge out both his eyes,
Or, if he found the chance, slaughter him,
And remove the child
Forever from this world.
His words concealed another purpose:
Hero Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
For the hero who would uphold the nation,
For the many Kyrgyz people in Talas,
For the champion who would be their support.
When mighty Kyyaz demanded him,
Aichürök burned and trembled;
She could not say, “I will not give him.”
Before the renowned hero Kyyaz’s
Overwhelming authority, Chürök’s
Life nearly left her then;
Her tiny soul shrieked,
And every bone in her body seemed to shatter.
What began in the morning lasted until evening.
If only I could return and see
Reedy Keng-Kol and Talas,
And take the young hero who remains of his khan
As my solace and support;
If only, in his old age, I could show Bakai,
And my mother in her declining years,
This token left by the hero,
Saying, “The young hero has come boldly home,”
If only I could let them see him once.
If only I could take my long-held vengeance
Upon the black-hearted choro,
And make the child my support—
How many dreadful thoughts she pondered.
Kyyaz has ten thousand, while we are few;
Will he cast him into a pit?
Will he rob the newborn infant
Of his sight in this world
And send him to his death?
The courageous woman Aichürök thought,
Rather than walk brightly, poor wretch,
Only to stand weeping in anguish,
I shall summon a hero’s courage.
Displaying the bearing of a warrior,
I shall save alive
My only refuge and excuse.
Though cast into fire, I shall not become ash;
Though plunged into misery, I shall not become a slave.
I shall make my words more forceful.
He means to tear me from my darling
And blind my eyes with grief;
May the doomed man be struck by God!
By tearing me from my only one,
He means to extinguish me like a fire.
God’s sun in the heavens grew dark,
And in poor Chürök’s mind
Sixty sorrows came at once.
Her heart was pierced and torn apart,
And Kyyaz, demanding, “Give me the child,”
Appeared in the guise of a dragon.
Seeing him, Chürök
Shed tears from her eyes.
The madman hero Kyyaz stood there,
Preparing to take the child;
If you had seen hero Kyyaz,
He raged like a blue lion.
Aichürök stood shrieking,
Tormented and distraught,
Yet betraying no suspicion to Kyyaz.
Her heart wandered and broke apart;
Unable to collect herself,
She shed tears from her eyes.
She could not wipe away her tears
Or draw back the mucus from her nose.
The dear bird called the kazgaldak
Flies over the plains without returning;
How much Aichürök had endured,
All for the child left by her khan.
